problem: Zero-shot object navigation methods (VLFM, ESC, OneMap) rely on 2D feature maps and greedily pick the single highest-scoring frontier, ignoring long-term planning. Others need extra training or heavy computation, which hurts complex scenes and real deployment.
motivation: Greedy frontier selection causes back-and-forth, inefficient search. Since search ends when the target is found, a TSP tour over all viewpoints (which minimizes total length) is also mismatched with the task. A formulation that prioritizes semantically likely viewpoints while planning globally should search more efficiently.
key_idea: Cast zero-shot object search as a Weighted Traveling Repairman Problem over frontier/detection/feature-match candidates, weighting each by VLM similarity so the tour minimizes weighted waiting time.
insight: Minimizing weighted cumulative arrival time (rather than tour length or greedy score) suits search that stops on finding the target, since it visits high-similarity, nearby candidates first while still planning globally. The multi-object ablation supports this: replacing WTRP with greedy drops SPL 23.0->17.1 and PPL 28.9->22.4, and a TSP exploration variant is much worse (SR 29.3). Re-checking detections lowers false positives, and patch-level CLIP maps beat image-level VLM scoring.
method: Semantic confidence map: patch-level CLIP similarity per pixel, projected with depth to a 2D grid (top-20% averaged), fused over time with a Kalman filter, with distance-decayed raycast into free space to score viewpoints.

3D feature map: patch-level CLIP embeddings stored in an octree voxel map; bilinear upsampling is merged into fusion via summed bilinear weights per voxel, which avoids high-dimensional interpolation; Kalman-fused, floor/ceiling removed, and matched against text queries.

Candidate generation: frontier-cluster viewpoints, YOLO-World detections (above tau_h become goals immediately, between tau_l and tau_h become candidates, and are re-checked over time), and 3D feature-map matches.

WTRP goal selection: node weight = alpha_s*exp(mu*S+nu) of similarity; cost matrix uses max(distance/v_max, yaw/omega_max), plus motion-consistency and small-enclosed-area terms for the first edge; solved with LKH; the first node is the mid-term goal, with replanning on arrival or timeout.
Local planner: A* waypoints, then MINCO trajectory optimization (adapted from swarm planner) and a low-level controller producing velocity commands.
Occupancy grid: Bayesian raycast update with inflation for navigation and frontier extraction.

setting.backbone: CLIP-based patch-level VLM (frozen, ConvNeXt-CLIP) + YOLO-World detector (frozen); LKH solver for planning
setting.action_space: continuous velocity commands (linear/angular) from trajectory optimization; A* waypoints

results: Single-object HM3D: 59.2 SR / 39.8 SPL, beating the training-free OneMap (55.8/37.4) and VLFM (52.5/30.4). Sequential multi-object: 57.2 SR / 33.4 SPL vs OneMap 54.2/27.8. Runs in real time on a Jetson Orin NX and was demonstrated on a real robot.
limitations: Evaluated only on HM3D in simulation with limited real-world qualitative demos and no quantitative real-world results
3D feature map is slow on embedded hardware (0.589 s vs 0.25 s desired interval)
Small gains in single-object; the text and table numbers are inconsistent; no ablation on the 3D map or on individual cost terms
